title: Comparing: -roq, eng, and clothes shopping
goal: Compare two things without a word for "more", name the best with *eng*, and shop for clothes in the right size.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Bu koʻylak menga toʻgʻri keladimi?
dialogs.intro: At a clothing store downtown. Budi is looking for a shirt for a friend's wedding.

lines.speaker: Sotuvchi:
lines.id: Welcome! What are you looking for?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I need a white shirt. I'm going to a wedding.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I don't know. In Indonesia I wear an M.

lines.speaker: Sotuvchi:
lines.text: Bu yerda oʻlchamlar kichikroq. L oling.
lines.id: Sizes here run smaller. Take an L.
lines.literal: this place-in sizes smaller. L take.

lines.speaker: Sotuvchi:
lines.text: Albatta, marhamat. Kiyinish xonasi u yerda.
lines.id: Of course, go ahead. The fitting room is over there.
lines.literal: of-course, please. dressing room-its that place-in.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bu yaxshiroq. Lekin qora rangi bormi?
lines.id: This is better. But do you have it in black?
lines.literal: this better. but black color-its exists-?

lines.speaker: Sotuvchi:
lines.text: Bor, ammo qoraroq koʻylak biroz qimmatroq.
lines.id: We do, but the black one is a bit more expensive.
lines.literal: exists, but blacker shirt a-bit more-expensive.

lines.speaker: Sotuvchi:
lines.text: Manavi — ikkinchi javondagi. Sifati ham yomon emas.
lines.id: This one — on the second shelf. The quality isn't bad either.
lines.literal: this-here — second shelf-on-the-one. quality-its also bad not.

notes: **-roq means "more", and there's no separate word for it.** *Katta* (big) → *kattaroq* (bigger). *Arzon* → *arzonroq*. Uzbek has no free-standing "more"; it all attaches — much like English "-er", but for every adjective.
**Toʻgʻri kelmoq = "to fit, to suit".** Literally "to come straight". *Bu menga toʻgʻri keladi* = this fits me. Another compound verb, and as usual you can't guess the meaning from its parts.

**Kiyib koʻrsam boʻladimi? = "may I try it on?"** The *-sa* inside it is the conditional form taught in unit 19. For now learn the pattern *…-sam boʻladimi?* as a whole — it's the most polite way to ask permission.
**Eng arzoni, not eng arzon.** When an adjective is used as a noun ("the cheapest one"), it gets the ending *-i*. Likewise *kattasi* (the big one), *yangisi* (the new one), *qizili* (the red one).

grammars.title: Three degrees of comparison
body: Uzbek comparison is built from two tools you already have: the ending *-roq*, and the "from" ending *-dan* from unit 8.

head: Degree
Form
Example
Meaning
rows: This is more expensive than that.
This is the most expensive shirt.
The most expensive one is this.

after: **The thing compared to takes -dan, not a word for "than".** *Sendan kattaman* = "I'm older than you" — literally "from-you big-I". Note that *-roq* can even be dropped here; *-dan* alone carries the comparison.
*Eng* is the only comparison word that stands on its own, and it always comes first: *eng yaxshi* (best), *eng katta* (biggest), *eng birinchi* (the very first).
For likeness, use *xuddi … kabi* or *-day/-dek*: *Bu xuddi u kabi* (this is just like that), *muzday sovuq* (cold as ice), *asalday shirin* (sweet as honey).

grammars.title: Ordinal numbers: -inchi
body: One ending turns every number into an ordinal. It's used for dates, floors, bus numbers, and school grades.
after: The rule: **number ending in a consonant → -inchi; ending in a vowel → -nchi.** *besh* → *beshinchi*, but *ikki* → *ikki**nchi***, *olti* → *olti**nchi***, *yetti* → *yetti**nchi***.
For dates, Uzbek puts **the month, then the day**: *mart oyining beshinchi kuni* or, shorter, *5-mart* (read *beshinchi mart*). The year: *2026-yil* (read *ikki ming yigirma oltinchi yil*).
*Birinchi* also means "first of all" at the start of a sentence: *Birinchi, non oling* = "first, take the bread".

blocks.text: Most of the words below are used with the verb *kiymoq* (to wear, to put on) — and like most definite objects, they need *-ni*: *koʻylakni kiying*.

A *doʻppi* is a black skullcap with white embroidery, worn by Uzbek men at formal events and on holidays. Its pattern varies by region — the one with four chili-pepper motifs comes from Chust in the Fergana Valley, and it's the most famous. Buying one is the most typical souvenir from Uzbekistan.

Useful sentences in a shop: *Oʻlchamingiz nechchi?* (what's your size), *Kattarogʻi bormi?* (do you have a bigger one?), *Bu menga toʻgʻri kelmadi* (this doesn't fit me), *Boshqa rangi bormi?* (do you have another color?).
Practice like this: pick two things around you, then make one comparison sentence for each row.
⚠️ *-roq* also attaches to adverbs: *sekinroq gapiring* (speak more slowly), *tezroq yuring* (walk faster), *keyinroq* (later). That last one is used all the time to put something off politely.
*Qulay* is one of the most useful words without a single English equivalent: it covers "comfortable", "convenient", and "a good time". *Sizga qachon qulay?* = "when suits you?"

items: Do you have a bigger one?
